title: Vertex-nonamenability implies linear range
statement:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be an infinite, connected, locally finite graph. For a finite set $S\subset V$, define its **outer vertex boundary** by

$$
\partial_V S=\{x\in V\setminus S:\ \exists\,y\in S\text{ with }x\sim y\}.
$$

The graph $G$ is **vertex-nonamenable** if

$$
\inf_{0<|S|<\infty}\frac{|\partial_V S|}{|S|}>0.
$$

For simple random walk $(X_t)_{t\geq 0}$ on $G$, let $R_t:=|\{X_0,\dots,X_t\}|$ denote its range.

**Vertex-nonamenability implies linear range.** If $G$ is vertex-nonamenable, then there exists $c=c(G)>0$ such that

$$
\forall t\geq 0,\qquad \mathbb{E}[R_t]\geq ct.
$$

On bounded-degree graphs, vertex-nonamenability implies a spectral gap and hence uniform transience, so the conjecture is already known in that setting. The open issue is whether the same conclusion holds for vertex-nonamenable graphs with unbounded degrees.
source_name: Itai Benjamini and Justin Salez, “How fast does the range of simple random walk grow?”, arXiv:2602.11051 (2026).
references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11051

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of February 2026).
